claim: p97 (also known as VCP, Cdc48) has crucial functions in protein quality control, organellar homeostasis, and DNA damage repair.
source: The ATPase p97 (also known as VCP, Cdc48) has crucial functions in a variety of important cellular processes such as protein quality control, organellar homeostasis, and DNA damage repair, and its de-regulation is linked to neuromuscular diseases and cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about p97 function and is referenced in the manuscript.

claim: De-regulation of p97 is linked to neuromuscular diseases and cancer.
source: The ATPase p97 (also known as VCP, Cdc48) has crucial functions in a variety of important cellular processes such as protein quality control, organellar homeostasis, and DNA damage repair, and its de-regulation is linked to neuromuscular diseases and cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the literature.

claim: FAM104 proteins are a conserved family of p97 interactors.
source: Here, we identify the hitherto uncharacterized FAM104 proteins as a conserved family of p97 interactors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from yeast two-hybrid screens and pulldown assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: VCF1 and VCF2 bind p97 directly via a novel, alpha-helical motif.
source: The two human family members VCP nuclear cofactor family member 1 and 2 (VCF1/2) bind p97 directly via a novel, alpha-helical motif and associate with p97-UFD1-NPL4 and p97-UBXN2B complexes in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct binding assays and structural modeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: VCF1/2 associate with p97-UFD1-NPL4 complexes in cells.
source: The two human family members VCP nuclear cofactor family member 1 and 2 (VCF1/2) bind p97 directly via a novel, alpha-helical motif and associate with p97-UFD1-NPL4 and p97-UBXN2B complexes in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: VCF1/2 associate with p97-UBXN2B complexes in cells.
source: The two human family members VCP nuclear cofactor family member 1 and 2 (VCF1/2) bind p97 directly via a novel, alpha-helical motif and associate with p97-UFD1-NPL4 and p97-UBXN2B complexes in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: VCF1/2 localize to the nucleus.
source: VCF1/2 localize to the nucleus and promote the nuclear import of p97.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: VCF1/2 promote the nuclear import of p97.
source: VCF1/2 localize to the nucleus and promote the nuclear import of p97.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy and fractionation experiments shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: Loss of VCF1/2 results in reduced nuclear p97 levels.
source: Loss of VCF1/2 results in reduced nuclear p97 levels, slow growth, and hypersensitivity to chemical inhibition of p97 in the absence and presence of DNA damage, suggesting that FAM104 proteins are critical regulators of nuclear p97 functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by knockout and knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Loss of VCF1/2 results in slow growth.
source: Loss of VCF1/2 results in reduced nuclear p97 levels, slow growth, and hypersensitivity to chemical inhibition of p97 in the absence and presence of DNA damage, suggesting that FAM104 proteins are critical regulators of nuclear p97 functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Loss of VCF1/2 results in hypersensitivity to chemical inhibition of p97 in the absence of DNA damage.
source: Loss of VCF1/2 results in reduced nuclear p97 levels, slow growth, and hypersensitivity to chemical inhibition of p97 in the absence and presence of DNA damage, suggesting that FAM104 proteins are critical regulators of nuclear p97 functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data with CB-5083 treatment shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Loss of VCF1/2 results in hypersensitivity to chemical inhibition of p97 in the presence of DNA damage.
source: Loss of VCF1/2 results in reduced nuclear p97 levels, slow growth, and hypersensitivity to chemical inhibition of p97 in the absence and presence of DNA damage, suggesting that FAM104 proteins are critical regulators of nuclear p97 functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data with camptothecin pretreatment and CB-5083 shown in Figure 7C.

claim: FAM104 proteins are critical regulators of nuclear p97 functions.
source: Loss of VCF1/2 results in reduced nuclear p97 levels, slow growth, and hypersensitivity to chemical inhibition of p97 in the absence and presence of DNA damage, suggesting that FAM104 proteins are critical regulators of nuclear p97 functions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing effects of VCF1/2 loss on nuclear p97 levels and cell fitness.

claim: p97 segregates ubiquitin-modified proteins in various protein quality control pathways for their subsequent degradation by the 26S proteasome.
source: The best-characterized function of p97 is the segregation of ubiquitin-modified proteins in various protein quality control pathways for their subsequent degradation by the 26S proteasome (Brandman et al., 2012; Dantuma and Hoppe, 2012; Tanaka et al., 2010; Ye et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: p97 is involved in the lysosomal degradation of endocytic cargo.
source: p97 is also involved in the lysosomal degradation of endocytic cargo (Ritz et al., 2011) and in the selective autophagy of protein aggregates, stress granules, as well as damaged mitochondria and lysosomes (Buchan et al., 2013; Ju et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2013; Papadopoulos et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2010; Turakhiya et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ritz et al., 2011.

claim: p97 is involved in the selective autophagy of protein aggregates, stress granules, as well as damaged mitochondria and lysosomes.
source: p97 is also involved in the lysosomal degradation of endocytic cargo (Ritz et al., 2011) and in the selective autophagy of protein aggregates, stress granules, as well as damaged mitochondria and lysosomes (Buchan et al., 2013; Ju et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2013; Papadopoulos et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2010; Turakhiya et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: p97 possesses crucial nuclear functions in DNA replication and DNA damage repair.
source: Moreover, p97 possesses a number of crucial nuclear functions, for instance, in DNA replication and DNA damage repair (Acs et al., 2011; Davis et al., 2012; Franz et al., 2011; Maric et al., 2014; Meerang et al., 2011; Moreno et al., 2014; Mosbech et al., 2012; Mouysset et al., 2008; Raman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Mutational perturbation of p97 function causes the neuromuscular degenerative disease multisystem proteinopathy 1 (MSP1).
source: Importantly, mutational perturbation of p97 function causes the neuromuscular degenerative disease multisystem proteinopathy 1 (MSP1) (Johnson et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2022; Watts et al., 2004), and several cancers as well as viral and bacterial pathogens rely on p97 activity, making p97 an attractive target for therapeutic intervention (Das and Dudley, 2021; Deshaies, 2014; Humphreys et al., 2009; Huryn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2022; Watts et al., 2004.

claim: Several cancers rely on p97 activity.
source: Importantly, mutational perturbation of p97 function causes the neuromuscular degenerative disease multisystem proteinopathy 1 (MSP1) (Johnson et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2022; Watts et al., 2004), and several cancers as well as viral and bacterial pathogens rely on p97 activity, making p97 an attractive target for therapeutic intervention (Das and Dudley, 2021; Deshaies, 2014; Humphreys et al., 2009; Huryn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Viral and bacterial pathogens rely on p97 activity.
source: Importantly, mutational perturbation of p97 function causes the neuromuscular degenerative disease multisystem proteinopathy 1 (MSP1) (Johnson et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2022; Watts et al., 2004), and several cancers as well as viral and bacterial pathogens rely on p97 activity, making p97 an attractive target for therapeutic intervention (Das and Dudley, 2021; Deshaies, 2014; Humphreys et al., 2009; Huryn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: p97 is an attractive target for therapeutic intervention.
source: Importantly, mutational perturbation of p97 function causes the neuromuscular degenerative disease multisystem proteinopathy 1 (MSP1) (Johnson et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2022; Watts et al., 2004), and several cancers as well as viral and bacterial pathogens rely on p97 activity, making p97 an attractive target for therapeutic intervention (Das and Dudley, 2021; Deshaies, 2014; Humphreys et al., 2009; Huryn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the role of p97 in diseases and is supported by citations.

claim: p97 unfolds substrate proteins by threading them through the ring-shaped p97 homohexamer in an ATP hydrolysis-driven process.
source: The molecular basis underlying the diverse cellular functions of p97 is the partial or complete unfolding of substrate proteins by threading through the ring-shaped p97 homohexamer in an ATP hydrolysis-driven process (Blythe et al., 2017; Bodnar and Rapoport, 2017; Buchberger, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blythe et al., 2017; Bodnar and Rapoport, 2017; Buchberger, 2022.

claim: p97 itself lacks appreciable specificity for its physiological substrates.
source: Since p97 itself lacks appreciable specificity for its physiological substrates, a large number of cofactor proteins control substrate binding, subcellular localization, and oligomeric state of p97 (reviewed in Buchberger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and citation to Buchberger et al., 2015.

claim: A large number of cofactor proteins control substrate binding, subcellular localization, and oligomeric state of p97.
source: Since p97 itself lacks appreciable specificity for its physiological substrates, a large number of cofactor proteins control substrate binding, subcellular localization, and oligomeric state of p97 (reviewed in Buchberger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Buchberger et al., 2015.

claim: UFD1-NPL4 recruits ubiquitylated substrates for p97-dependent unfolding and subsequent proteasomal degradation or processing.
source: a heterodimer of UFD1 (also known as UFD1L) and NPL4 (also known as NPLOC4) recruits ubiquitylated substrates for p97-dependent unfolding and subsequent proteasomal degradation or processing (Bays et al., 2001; Jarosch et al., 2002; Rape et al., 2001; Ye et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bays et al., 2001; Jarosch et al., 2002; Rape et al., 2001; Ye et al., 2001.

claim: UBXN6 controls p97 functions in lysosomal and autophagic degradation pathways.
source: whereas UBXN6 (also known as UBXD1) controls p97 functions in lysosomal and autophagic degradation pathways (Papadopoulos et al., 2017; Ritz et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Papadopoulos et al., 2017; Ritz et al., 2011.

claim: SEP domain-containing cofactors such as p47 and UBXN2B mediate the maturation of protein phosphatase 1 complexes.
source: and SEP domain-containing cofactors such as p47 (also known as NSFL1C) and UBXN2B (also known as p37) mediate the maturation of protein phosphatase 1 complexes (Weith et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weith et al., 2018.

claim: Ubx2 recruits Cdc48-Ufd1-Npl4 to the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria to promote ER- and outer mitochondrial membrane-associated protein degradation.
source: For example, the yeast cofactor Ubx2 recruits Cdc48-Ufd1-Npl4 to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria to promote ER- and outer mitochondrial membrane-associated protein degradation, respectively (Mårtensson et al., 2019; Neuber et al., 2005; Schuberth and Buchberger, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mårtensson et al., 2019; Neuber et al., 2005; Schuberth and Buchberger, 2005.

claim: UBXN7 and FAF1 direct p97-UFD1-NPL4 to nuclear chromatin to promote the removal of ubiquitylated substrates such as CDT1 and the CMG helicase.
source: Similarly, the metazoan cofactors UBXN7 and FAF1 direct p97-UFD1-NPL4 to nuclear chromatin to promote the removal of ubiquitylated substrates such as CDT1 and the CMG helicase (Franz et al., 2016b; Fujisawa et al., 2022; Kochenova et al., 2022; Tarcan et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Franz et al., 2016b; Fujisawa et al., 2022; Kochenova et al., 2022; Tarcan et al., 2022.

claim: The majority of cofactors interact with p97 through a small number of defined domains/motifs, including the UBX(-like) domain, the PUB and PUL domains, the SHP box, the VCP interacting motif (VIM), and the VCP binding motif (VBM).
source: The majority of cofactors interact with p97 through a small number of defined domains/motifs, including the UBX(-like) domain, the PUB and PUL domains, the SHP box, the VCP interacting motif (VIM), and the VCP binding motif (VBM) (reviewed in Buchberger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Buchberger et al., 2015.

claim: Some p97 interactors do not possess any of the canonical binding motifs.
source: However, some p97 interactors do not possess any of these canonical binding motifs, suggesting that the current inventory of p97 cofactors is incomplete and, hence, that the full scope of the p97–cofactor network is far from being understood.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that some interactors lack known motifs.

claim: The current inventory of p97 cofactors is incomplete.
source: However, some p97 interactors do not possess any of these canonical binding motifs, suggesting that the current inventory of p97 cofactors is incomplete and, hence, that the full scope of the p97–cofactor network is far from being understood.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the existence of interactors without canonical motifs.

claim: ZFAND1 regulates p97 functions in stress granule clearance.
source: Examples illustrating this point include ZFAND1 (yeast Cuz1) and GIGYF1/2 (yeast Smy2), which were recently shown to regulate p97 functions in stress granule clearance (Turakhiya et al., 2018) and the transcription stress response (Lehner et al., 2022), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Turakhiya et al., 2018.

claim: GIGYF1/2 regulates p97 functions in the transcription stress response.
source: Examples illustrating this point include ZFAND1 (yeast Cuz1) and GIGYF1/2 (yeast Smy2), which were recently shown to regulate p97 functions in stress granule clearance (Turakhiya et al., 2018) and the transcription stress response (Lehner et al., 2022), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lehner et al., 2022.

claim: Multiple clones encoding FAM104A and FAM104B were isolated in a yeast two-hybrid screen of a human testis cDNA library.
source: In our ongoing efforts to identify p97 binding partners, we isolated multiple clones encoding the hitherto uncharacterized proteins FAM104A (also known as FLJ14775) and FAM104B (also known as FLJ20434, CXorf44) in a yeast two-hybrid screen of a human testis cDNA library (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the yeast two-hybrid screen.

claim: VCF1 and VCF2 are both expressed in various isoforms originating from alternative transcript variants.
source: VCF1 and 2 are both expressed in various isoforms originating from alternative transcript variants (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the schematic representation in Figure 1A showing different isoforms.

claim: For VCF1, the two-hybrid hits matched isoforms 1, 2, and 5.
source: For VCF1, the two-hybrid hits matched isoforms 1, 2, and 5, whereas isoforms 3 and 4, which share just the N-terminal 73 residues with isoforms 1/2, were not isolated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast two-hybrid screening data.

claim: VCF1 isoforms 3 and 4 were not isolated in the two-hybrid screen.
source: For VCF1, the two-hybrid hits matched isoforms 1, 2, and 5, whereas isoforms 3 and 4, which share just the N-terminal 73 residues with isoforms 1/2, were not isolated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast two-hybrid screening data.

claim: For VCF2, the two-hybrid hits matched isoforms 3 and 4/5/6.
source: For VCF2, the two-hybrid hits matched isoforms 3 and 4/5/6, respectively, which differ by the insertion of a single valine residue after residue 40.
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast two-hybrid screening data.

claim: VCF2 isoforms 3 and 4/5/6 differ by the insertion of a single valine residue after residue 40.
source: For VCF2, the two-hybrid hits matched isoforms 3 and 4/5/6, respectively, which differ by the insertion of a single valine residue after residue 40.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of the isolated clones.

claim: VCF2 isoforms 1 and 2 were not isolated in the two-hybrid screen.
source: Isoforms 1 and 2, which possess 30 divergent C-terminal residues, and isoform 7, which is truncated after 46 residues, were not isolated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast two-hybrid screening data.

claim: VCF2 isoform 7 was not isolated in the two-hybrid screen.
source: Isoforms 1 and 2, which possess 30 divergent C-terminal residues, and isoform 7, which is truncated after 46 residues, were not isolated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast two-hybrid screening data.

claim: The isoforms of VCF1 and 2 that were isolated in the two-hybrid screen possess significant sequence homology.
source: Of note, those isoforms of VCF1 and 2 that were isolated in the two-hybrid screen possess significant sequence homology, suggesting that they are evolutionarily related.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: VCF1 and VCF2 are evolutionarily related.
source: Of note, those isoforms of VCF1 and 2 that were isolated in the two-hybrid screen possess significant sequence homology, suggesting that they are evolutionarily related.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the sequence homology data.

claim: FAM104-like proteins are present in vertebrates as well as in many invertebrates, including insects, octopuses, and echinodermata.
source: Indeed, FAM104-like proteins are present in vertebrates as well as in many invertebrates, including insects, octopuses, and echinodermata, whereas the occurrence of two distinct, VCF1- and VCF2-like homologs appears to be restricted to mammals (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The occurrence of two distinct, VCF1- and VCF2-like homologs appears to be restricted to mammals.
source: Indeed, FAM104-like proteins are present in vertebrates as well as in many invertebrates, including insects, octopuses, and echinodermata, whereas the occurrence of two distinct, VCF1- and VCF2-like homologs appears to be restricted to mammals (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FAM104 family members possess a predicted mono- or bipartite classical nuclear localization signal (cNLS) at or close to the N terminus.
source: Basically, FAM104 family members possess a predicted mono- or bipartite classical nuclear localization signal (cNLS) at or close to the N terminus and a C-terminal, highly conserved helical region, which are separated by largely unstructured stretches of variable length and lower sequence conservation (Figure 1A and B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and prediction shown in Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FAM104 family members possess a C-terminal, highly conserved helical region.
source: Basically, FAM104 family members possess a predicted mono- or bipartite classical nuclear localization signal (cNLS) at or close to the N terminus and a C-terminal, highly conserved helical region, which are separated by largely unstructured stretches of variable length and lower sequence conservation (Figure 1A and B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The cNLS and C-terminal helical region of FAM104 proteins are separated by largely unstructured stretches of variable length and lower sequence conservation.
source: Basically, FAM104 family members possess a predicted mono- or bipartite classical nuclear localization signal (cNLS) at or close to the N terminus and a C-terminal, highly conserved helical region, which are separated by largely unstructured stretches of variable length and lower sequence conservation (Figure 1A and B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: VCF1 isoforms 1, 2, and 5 interact with p97 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: To validate the results of the two-hybrid screen, we tested isoforms 1, 2, and 5 of VCF1 and isoform 3 of VCF2 in directed yeast two-hybrid assays and confirmed that all four full-length proteins interact with p97 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VCF2 isoform 3 interacts with p97 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: To validate the results of the two-hybrid screen, we tested isoforms 1, 2, and 5 of VCF1 and isoform 3 of VCF2 in directed yeast two-hybrid assays and confirmed that all four full-length proteins interact with p97 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GST fusions of VCF1 isoforms 1, 2, and 5 and VCF2 isoform 3 efficiently bind recombinant p97.
source: Next, we performed glutathione sepharose pulldown experiments with purified GST fusions of these four VCF1/2 proteins and found that they were all able to efficiently bind recombinant p97 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The N domain of p97 is necessary and sufficient for the direct binding of p97 to VCF1/2.
source: The ND1 variant of p97 lacking the D2 ATPase domain as well as the N domain alone bound efficiently to VCF1 and 2, whereas the ΔN variant lacking the N domain did not. Taken together, these results show that FAM104 proteins are a new family of evolutionarily conserved p97 interactors, and that the N domain is necessary and sufficient for the direct binding of p97 to VCF1/2.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown assay data with p97 truncation variants shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The p97 ND1 variant lacking the D2 ATPase domain binds efficiently to VCF1 and VCF2.
source: The ND1 variant of p97 lacking the D2 ATPase domain as well as the N domain alone bound efficiently to VCF1 and 2, whereas the ΔN variant lacking the N domain did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The N domain alone of p97 binds efficiently to VCF1 and VCF2.
source: The ND1 variant of p97 lacking the D2 ATPase domain as well as the N domain alone bound efficiently to VCF1 and 2, whereas the ΔN variant lacking the N domain did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The p97 ΔN variant lacking the N domain does not bind to VCF1 and VCF2.
source: The ND1 variant of p97 lacking the D2 ATPase domain as well as the N domain alone bound efficiently to VCF1 and 2, whereas the ΔN variant lacking the N domain did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The shortest VCF1 fragment isolated in the two-hybrid screen starts at glycine residue G131 of isoform 1.
source: The shortest VCF1 fragment isolated in the two-hybrid screen starts at glycine residue G131 of isoform 1 (equivalent to G110 and G64 of isoforms 2 and 5, respectively).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the two-hybrid screening results.

claim: Deletion of the four C-terminal residues of VCF1 isoform 5 does not affect the two-hybrid interaction with p97.
source: While deletion of the four C-terminal residues did not affect the two-hybrid interaction between VCF1 isoform 5 and p97, larger deletions of 7–26 residues completely abolished p97 binding (Figure 2B), even though the truncated proteins were expressed to similar levels in the reporter yeast strain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Larger C-terminal deletions of 7–26 residues in VCF1 isoform 5 completely abolish p97 binding in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: While deletion of the four C-terminal residues did not affect the two-hybrid interaction between VCF1 isoform 5 and p97, larger deletions of 7–26 residues completely abolished p97 binding (Figure 2B), even though the truncated proteins were expressed to similar levels in the reporter yeast strain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2B and expression data in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of the C-terminal 26 residues impairs the ability of all four VCF1/2 isoforms to bind p97 in pulldown experiments.
source: Consistent with this, deletion of the C-terminal 26 residues impaired the ability of all four VCF1/2 isoforms to bind p97 in a pulldown experiment (Figure 2D), indicating that the C-terminal region contains the p97 binding site.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The C-terminal region of VCF1/2 contains the p97 binding site.
source: Consistent with this, deletion of the C-terminal 26 residues impaired the ability of all four VCF1/2 isoforms to bind p97 in a pulldown experiment (Figure 2D), indicating that the C-terminal region contains the p97 binding site.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the deletion mapping data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A peptide spanning residues C180 to G203 of VCF1 isoform 1 can bind to p97.
source: We therefore tested whether a peptide spanning the conserved alpha-helical and flanking residues (residues C180 to G203 in VCF1 isoform 1) can bind to p97. To that end, we immobilized the N-terminally biotinylated peptide on streptavidin sepharose beads and performed a pulldown assay with p97 (Figure 2E). The peptide pulled down full-length p97 as well as the ND1 and N domain variants, demonstrating that the C-terminal conserved region of FAM104 family proteins is not only necessary, but also sufficient for p97 binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by peptide pulldown assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The C-terminal conserved region of FAM104 family proteins is not only necessary, but also sufficient for p97 binding.
source: The peptide pulled down full-length p97 as well as the ND1 and N domain variants, demonstrating that the C-terminal conserved region of FAM104 family proteins is not only necessary, but also sufficient for p97 binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by peptide pulldown assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The VCF1-derived peptide has some weak affinity for a p97 region(s) outside the N domain.
source: We also noted some residual binding of the p97 ΔN variant, suggesting that the VCF1-derived peptide has some weak affinity for a p97 region(s) outside the N domain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of residual binding in Figure 2E.

claim: The subdomain cleft of the p97 N domain is the major binding site for other N domain binding motifs including the UBX(-like) domain and the VIM and VBM linear motifs.
source: The central part of the C-terminal region was predicted as an alpha-helix that binds to the subdomain cleft of the p97 N domain (Figure 2F), which is the major binding site for other N domain binding motifs including the UBX(-like) domain and the VIM and VBM linear motifs (Buchberger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Buchberger et al., 2015.

claim: The four most strongly conserved residues of the VCF1 C-terminal helix (Y184, N188, L191, and H195) all contact the p97 N domain.
source: Closer inspection of the modeled interface revealed that the four most strongly conserved residues of the helix, Y184, N188, L191, and H195, all contact the N domain (Figure 2G; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by AlphaFold Multimer structural modeling shown in Figure 2G.

claim: L191 of VCF1 occupies a predominantly hydrophobic pocket in the p97 subdomain cleft.
source: The predicted interactions are centered around L191, which occupies a predominantly hydrophobic pocket in the p97 subdomain cleft.
evidence: This claim is supported by AlphaFold Multimer structural modeling shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Y184 of VCF1 is predicted to exhibit an orthogonal pi-stacking with Y138 of p97.
source: Adjacent residues contribute to a hydrogen bonding network with p97, while Y184 is predicted to exhibit an orthogonal pi-stacking with Y138 of p97.
evidence: This claim is supported by AlphaFold Multimer structural modeling shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The N188A/L191A double mutation in VCF1 abolishes the interaction with p97.
source: Intriguingly, both double mutations abolished the interaction of VCF1 with p97 as efficiently as the deletion of the entire C-terminal region (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The N188R/L191R double mutation in VCF1 abolishes the interaction with p97.
source: Intriguingly, both double mutations abolished the interaction of VCF1 with p97 as efficiently as the deletion of the entire C-terminal region (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Residues N188 and L191 are of central importance for the interaction between VCF1 and p97.
source: Together, our data identify the C-terminal alpha-helix of FAM104 proteins as a novel p97 binding motif and show that the strictly conserved residues N188 and L191 are of central importance for the interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The C-terminal alpha-helix of FAM104 proteins is a novel p97 binding motif.
source: Together, our data identify the C-terminal alpha-helix of FAM104 proteins as a novel p97 binding motif and show that the strictly conserved residues N188 and L191 are of central importance for the interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data from deletion mapping, peptide binding, structural modeling, and mutagenesis.

claim: An AlphaFold Multimer model of the Drosophila melanogaster homologs of VCF1/2 (CG14229) and p97 (TER94) shows a highly similar binding interface to the human proteins.
source: Consistent with a conserved essential role of residues N188 and L191 for p97 binding, an AlphaFold Multimer model of the Drosophila melanogaster homologs of VCF1/2 (CG14229) and p97 (TER94) showed a highly similar binding interface with basically identical positions of the equivalent residues N90 and L93 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by AlphaFold Multimer structural modeling shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenous p97 is efficiently co-precipitated with all four wild-type VCF1/2 proteins tested in anti-FLAG immunoprecipitations.
source: Endogenous p97 was efficiently co-precipitated with all four wild-type VCF1/2 proteins tested, despite the fact that VCF1 isoform 5 was less and VCF2 isoform 3 was much less well expressed than VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2, and that the levels of soluble p97 in the input were strongly reduced upon ectopic expression of VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: UFD1 and NPL4 are co-precipitated with VCF1/2 at levels roughly proportional to those of p97.
source: Importantly, UFD1 and NPL4 were co-precipitated at levels roughly proportional to those of p97, strongly suggesting that VCP1/2 form complexes with p97-UFD1-NPL4.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: VCF1/2 form complexes with p97-UFD1-NPL4.
source: Importantly, UFD1 and NPL4 were co-precipitated at levels roughly proportional to those of p97, strongly suggesting that VCP1/2 form complexes with p97-UFD1-NPL4.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: VCF1 Cdel26 variants lacking the C-terminal helix fail to co-precipitate p97, UFD1, and NPL4.
source: This conclusion is further supported by the finding that VCF1 Cdel26 variants lacking the C-terminal helix failed to co-precipitate not only p97, as expected, but also UFD1 and NPL4.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: UBXN2B is robustly co-precipitated with wild-type VCF1/2 proteins.
source: We also detected a robust co-precipitation of the SEP domain cofactor UBXN2B with the wild-type, but not Cdel26 VCF1/2 proteins (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating the existence of ternary p97-UBXN2B-VCF1/2 complexes and thereby confirming and extending recent data from high-throughput interaction studies (Huttlin et al., 2017; Luck et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: UBXN2B is not co-precipitated with Cdel26 VCF1/2 proteins.
source: We also detected a robust co-precipitation of the SEP domain cofactor UBXN2B with the wild-type, but not Cdel26 VCF1/2 proteins (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating the existence of ternary p97-UBXN2B-VCF1/2 complexes and thereby confirming and extending recent data from high-throughput interaction studies (Huttlin et al., 2017; Luck et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Ternary p97-UBXN2B-VCF1/2 complexes exist.
source: We also detected a robust co-precipitation of the SEP domain cofactor UBXN2B with the wild-type, but not Cdel26 VCF1/2 proteins (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating the existence of ternary p97-UBXN2B-VCF1/2 complexes and thereby confirming and extending recent data from high-throughput interaction studies (Huttlin et al., 2017; Luck et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data and supported by citations to Huttlin et al., 2017; Luck et al., 2020.

claim: FAF1 and UBXN7 are co-precipitated with VCF1/2.
source: Interestingly, FAF1 and UBXN7, two auxiliary cofactors important for nuclear functions of p97-UFD1-NPL4, were also co-precipitated with VCF1/2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The N-terminal extension shared by VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2 mediates a direct interaction with FAF1.
source: These results suggest that the N-terminal extension shared by VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2 mediates a direct interaction with FAF1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential binding of FAF1 to different VCF1 isoforms shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: All four VCF1/2 proteins strongly accumulate in the nucleus when ectopically expressed in HeLa cells.
source: Consistent with the very high score calculated by cNLS mapper (Kosugi et al., 2009), all four VCF1/2 proteins strongly accumulated in the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Endogenous p97 co-accumulates with ectopically expressed VCF1/2 in the nuclei of transfected cells.
source: Intriguingly, endogenous p97 co-accumulated with VCF1/2 in the nuclei of transfected cells, as evident from the comparison with neighboring non-transfected cells or with the vector control (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: C-terminally truncated VCF1 Cdel26 variants localize to the nucleus but fail to effectuate a significant nuclear accumulation of p97.
source: The C-terminally truncated VCF1 Cdel26 variants localized to the nucleus but failed to effectuate a significant nuclear accumulation of p97, as expected from the loss of their p97 binding site.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and quantification in Figure 4C.

claim: cNLS-deleted VCF1 variants show a nuclear and cytoplasmic distribution.
source: The cNLS-deleted VCF1 variants showed a nuclear and cytoplasmic distribution, in accordance with their small size of less than 40 kDa, and a much less pronounced nuclear accumulation of p97 (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1A for higher intensity images of full-length versus cNLS-deleted VCF1 isoform 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: cNLS-deleted VCF1 variants cause a much less pronounced nuclear accumulation of p97 compared to wild-type VCF1.
source: The cNLS-deleted VCF1 variants showed a nuclear and cytoplasmic distribution, in accordance with their small size of less than 40 kDa, and a much less pronounced nuclear accumulation of p97 (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1A for higher intensity images of full-length versus cNLS-deleted VCF1 isoform 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B, C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic p97 signal increases strongly from 2.08 ± 0.01 for control-transfected cells to up to 15.46 ± 3.21 for cells transfected with wild-type VCF1 isoform 1.
source: The ratio increased strongly from 2.08 ± 0.01 for control-transfected cells to up to 15.46 ± 3.21 for cells transfected with wild-type VCF1 isoform 1, reflecting the robust nuclear accumulation of p97 in the presence of VCF1/2.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No significant nuclear accumulation of p97 is observed for cells transfected with the Cdel26 or the cNLS-deleted VCF1 variants.
source: By contrast, no significant nuclear accumulation of p97 was observed for cells transfected with the Cdel26 or the cNLS-deleted VCF1 variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Wild-type and Cdel26 VCF1/2 proteins strongly accumulate in the nucleus.
source: Quantification of the FLAG signals showed that the wild-type and Cdel26 VCF1/2 proteins strongly accumulated in the nucleus, whereas the cNLS-deleted variants were detected in both cytoplasm and nucleus (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: cNLS-deleted VCF1 variants are detected in both cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: Quantification of the FLAG signals showed that the wild-type and Cdel26 VCF1/2 proteins strongly accumulated in the nucleus, whereas the cNLS-deleted variants were detected in both cytoplasm and nucleus (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: VCF1/2 target p97 via a piggy-back mechanism to the nucleus.
source: Together, these results suggest that VCF1/2 target p97 via a piggy-back mechanism to the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data showing that VCF1/2 nuclear localization depends on their cNLS and that they recruit p97 to the nucleus via their C-terminal helix.

claim: Overexpression of VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2 causes a strong increase of p97 in the chromatin fraction at the expense of the cytoplasmic pool.
source: Intriguingly, the overexpression of both VCF1 isoforms did not affect the total amount of p97, as judged by the signal in SDS-denatured total cell extracts, but caused a strong increase of p97 in the chromatin fraction at the expense of the cytoplasmic pool.
evidence: This claim is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Overexpression of VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2 does not affect the total amount of p97.
source: Intriguingly, the overexpression of both VCF1 isoforms did not affect the total amount of p97, as judged by the signal in SDS-denatured total cell extracts, but caused a strong increase of p97 in the chromatin fraction at the expense of the cytoplasmic pool.
evidence: This claim is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The majority of p97 is released into the solubilized chromatin fraction upon benzonase treatment in cells overexpressing VCF1 isoform 1.
source: Comparing cells overexpressing VCF1 isoform 1 with control cells, we found that the majority of p97 was released into the solubilized chromatin fraction upon benzonase treatment, similar to VCF1 isoform 1 itself and the chromatin-associated proteins MYC, MCM7, and Ub-H2B.
evidence: This claim is supported by fractionation data with benzonase treatment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2 strongly associate with chromatin upon overexpression.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2 strongly associate with chromatin, at least upon overexpression, thereby inducing chromatin binding of p97, and they provide a rationale for the reduction of soluble p97 observed in the immunoprecipitation experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2 induce chromatin binding of p97 upon overexpression.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2 strongly associate with chromatin, at least upon overexpression, thereby inducing chromatin binding of p97, and they provide a rationale for the reduction of soluble p97 observed in the immunoprecipitation experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: VCF1 knockout and VCF1/2 double-knockout HeLa cell pools show a significantly reduced nuclear p97 signal compared to control cells.
source: Compared to control cells, both knockout cell pools showed a significantly reduced nuclear p97 signal, with the ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic p97 decreased by about 22% (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and quantification in Figure 6C.

claim: The ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic p97 is decreased by about 22% in VCF1 knockout and VCF1/2 double-knockout HeLa cell pools.
source: Compared to control cells, both knockout cell pools showed a significantly reduced nuclear p97 signal, with the ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic p97 decreased by about 22% (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: siRNA-mediated depletion of VCF1 reduces nuclear p97 levels.
source: The siRNA-mediated depletion of VCF1 had a similar effect (Figure 6B and D), which was more obvious to the naked eye in maximum intensity projections of z stacks (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6B and quantification in Figure 6D.

claim: A comparable reduction in nuclear p97 is observed in VCF1 single and VCF1/2 double-knockout HEK293T cell pools.
source: Moreover, a comparable reduction in nuclear p97 was observed in VCF1 single and VCF1/2 double-knockout HEK293T cell pools (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and quantification in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: High-content microscopy of VCF1/2 double-knockout HeLa cells shows a statistically highly significant reduction of the ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic p97 by 25%.
source: To further confirm these results, we used high-content microscopy of control and VCF1/2 double-knockout HeLa cells and found a statistically highly significant reduction of the ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic p97 by 25% (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), in excellent agreement with the confocal microscopy analyses.
evidence: This claim is supported by high-content microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The doxycycline-induced expression of NLS-FLAG-p97 increases the nuclear p97 signal to the same levels in VCF1-depleted and control-depleted cells.
source: Intriguingly, the doxycycline-induced expression of NLS-FLAG-p97 increased the nuclear p97 signal to the same levels in the VCF1-depleted and control-depleted cells, thereby fully compensating for the lack of VCF1.
evidence: This claim is supported by high-content microscopy data shown in Figure 6E and quantification in Figure 6F.

claim: Expression of NLS-FLAG-p97 fully compensates for the lack of VCF1 with respect to nuclear p97 localization.
source: Intriguingly, the doxycycline-induced expression of NLS-FLAG-p97 increased the nuclear p97 signal to the same levels in the VCF1-depleted and control-depleted cells, thereby fully compensating for the lack of VCF1.
evidence: This claim is supported by high-content microscopy data shown in Figure 6E and quantification in Figure 6F.

claim: Endogenous VCF1/2 modulate the nucleo-cytoplasmic distribution of p97.
source: In summary, our data show that endogenous VCF1/2 modulate the nucleo-cytoplasmic distribution of p97, and that the presence of a strong cNLS at p97 either in trans (via binding of VCF1/2) or in cis (via an N-terminal fusion) is necessary for the efficient nuclear localization of p97.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data from knockout, knockdown, and rescue experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The presence of a strong cNLS at p97 either in trans (via binding of VCF1/2) or in cis (via an N-terminal fusion) is necessary for the efficient nuclear localization of p97.
source: In summary, our data show that endogenous VCF1/2 modulate the nucleo-cytoplasmic distribution of p97, and that the presence of a strong cNLS at p97 either in trans (via binding of VCF1/2) or in cis (via an N-terminal fusion) is necessary for the efficient nuclear localization of p97.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data from knockout, knockdown, and rescue experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The number of VCF1/2 double-knockout cells is reduced by more than 40% compared to control cells eight days after seeding.
source: Eight days after seeding equal numbers of cells, the number of knockout cells was reduced by more than 40% compared to control cells, indicating that VCF1/2 are required for normal growth under otherwise unperturbed conditions (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: VCF1/2 are required for normal growth under otherwise unperturbed conditions.
source: Eight days after seeding equal numbers of cells, the number of knockout cells was reduced by more than 40% compared to control cells, indicating that VCF1/2 are required for normal growth under otherwise unperturbed conditions (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the growth assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Growth of VCF1/2 double-knockout cells is significantly impaired in the presence of 100 and 200 nM CB-5083.
source: While no statistically significant growth difference between knockout and control cells was observed at lower CB-5083 concentrations, growth of the knockout cells was significantly impaired in the presence of 100 and 200 nM CB-5083, indicating that loss of VCF1/2 made the cells hypersensitive to p97 inhibition (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data with CB-5083 treatment shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Loss of VCF1/2 makes cells hypersensitive to p97 inhibition.
source: While no statistically significant growth difference between knockout and control cells was observed at lower CB-5083 concentrations, growth of the knockout cells was significantly impaired in the presence of 100 and 200 nM CB-5083, indicating that loss of VCF1/2 made the cells hypersensitive to p97 inhibition (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the growth assay data with CB-5083 treatment shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Overexpression of VCF1 isoform 1 causes slightly reduced growth and enhanced CB-5083 sensitivity.
source: We also tested the effect of VCF1 overexpression by transiently transfecting HEK293T cells with the strongly expressed isoform 1 and observed slightly reduced growth and enhanced CB-5083 sensitivity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A balanced expression of VCF1/2 is crucial for optimal p97 function.
source: This negative effect on cellular fitness is consistent with the strong impact of VCF1 isoform1 overexpression on cofactor binding to p97 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that a balanced expression of VCF1/2 is crucial for optimal p97 function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on overexpression effects and cofactor binding.

claim: VCF1/2 double-knockout cells show a trend towards reduced growth in the presence of CB-5083 after camptothecin pretreatment.
source: By contrast, a clear trend towards reduced growth was observed for the knockout cells in the presence of CB-5083. While this effect did not reach statistical significance at all CB-5083 concentrations, it did so at 25 nM, that is, at a concentration that had no effect in the absence of camptothecin pretreatment (see Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data with camptothecin pretreatment shown in Figure 7C.

claim: VCF1/2 are required for optimal cell fitness, particularly under conditions of limited p97 activity.
source: Together, these results show that VCF1/2 are required for optimal cell fitness, particularly under conditions of limited p97 activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined growth assay data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: The expression of VCF1 is induced by 1.75- to 2-fold upon CB-5083 treatment for 24 hr.
source: The expression of VCF1 was induced by 1.75- to 2-fold upon CB-5083 treatment, suggesting that cells try to compensate impaired p97 function by increased VCF1 levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cells try to compensate impaired p97 function by increased VCF1 levels.
source: The expression of VCF1 was induced by 1.75- to 2-fold upon CB-5083 treatment, suggesting that cells try to compensate impaired p97 function by increased VCF1 levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the qRT-PCR data showing VCF1 upregulation upon p97 inhibition shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Treatment of control cells with 1 µM CB-5083 for 6 hr leads to an accumulation of small cytoplasmic p97-positive puncta and a significant decrease in the ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic p97 signal to 79%.
source: Intriguingly, treatment of control cells with 1 µM CB-5083 for 6 hr or with 0.5 µM CB-5083 for 24 hr led to an accumulation of small cytoplasmic p97-positive puncta and to a significant decrease in the ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic p97 signal to 79 and 72%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7E and quantification in Figure 7F.

claim: Treatment of control cells with 0.5 µM CB-5083 for 24 hr leads to an accumulation of small cytoplasmic p97-positive puncta and a significant decrease in the ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic p97 signal to 72%.
source: Intriguingly, treatment of control cells with 1 µM CB-5083 for 6 hr or with 0.5 µM CB-5083 for 24 hr led to an accumulation of small cytoplasmic p97-positive puncta and to a significant decrease in the ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic p97 signal to 79 and 72%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7E and quantification in Figure 7F.

claim: CB-5083 treatment decreases the nuclear p97 signal of VCF1/2 knockout cells to 67% (1 µM, 6 hr) and 65% (0.5 µM, 24 hr).
source: Importantly, CB-5083 treatment decreased the already reduced nuclear p97 signal of the VCF1/2 knockout cells even further to 67 and 65%, demonstrating that the effects of p97 inhibition and lack of VCF1/2 on the nuclear localization of p97 are additive.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7E and quantification in Figure 7F.

claim: The effects of p97 inhibition and lack of VCF1/2 on the nuclear localization of p97 are additive.
source: Importantly, CB-5083 treatment decreased the already reduced nuclear p97 signal of the VCF1/2 knockout cells even further to 67 and 65%, demonstrating that the effects of p97 inhibition and lack of VCF1/2 on the nuclear localization of p97 are additive.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7E and quantification in Figure 7F.

claim: The combined VCF1/2 deletion and inhibitor treatment reduces nuclear p97 levels and functions to an extent that is no longer compatible with viability.
source: Together with the synthetic growth defects described above, these results strongly suggest that the combined VCF1/2 deletion and inhibitor treatment reduces nuclear p97 levels and functions to an extent that is no longer compatible with viability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on growth defects and nuclear p97 localization shown in Figure 7.

claim: The position of the VCF1 helix in the AlphaFold model is similar to those of the helical VIM and VBM p97 binding motifs.
source: Interestingly, the position of the VCF1 helix in the model is similar to those of the helical VIM and VBM p97 binding motifs in the absence of any significant sequence similarity (Buchberger et al., 2015; Hänzelmann and Schindelin, 2011; Lim et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of structural models and is supported by citations.

claim: The key p97-contacting residues in VCF1 (N188 and L191) are distinct from those in VIM and VBM (predominantly arginine residues).
source: Even the respective key p97-contacting residues are distinct, with N188 and L191 in the C-terminal helix of VCF1 versus predominantly arginine residues in VIM and VBM.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of structural models and sequence analysis.

claim: Alpha-helices can efficiently bind to the N subdomain cleft of p97 via just one or two key residues.
source: The finding that alpha-helices can efficiently bind to the N subdomain cleft via just one or two key residues underlines the plasticity of this binding interface and raises the intriguing possibility that additional interactors bind p97 through yet other helical motifs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural analysis of VCF1 binding and comparison with other motifs.

claim: Additional interactors may bind p97 through yet other helical motifs.
source: The finding that alpha-helices can efficiently bind to the N subdomain cleft via just one or two key residues underlines the plasticity of this binding interface and raises the intriguing possibility that additional interactors bind p97 through yet other helical motifs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed plasticity of the p97 N domain binding interface.

claim: The strongly expressed VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2 efficiently outcompete the major cofactors UFD1-NPL4 and p47 as well as high molecular weight ubiquitin species.
source: Intriguingly, the strongly expressed VCF1 isoforms 1 and 2 efficiently outcompeted the major cofactors UFD1-NPL4 and p47 as well as high molecular weight ubiquitin species presumably representing polyubiquitylated substrate proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The more weakly expressed VCF1 isoform 5 and VCF2 isoform 3 do not interfere with binding of UFD1-NPL4 and p47.
source: By contrast, the more weakly expressed VCF1 isoform 5 and VCF2 isoform 3 did not interfere with binding of UFD1-NPL4 and p47 and even appeared to increase the association of ubiquitylated substrates with p97.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: VCF1 isoform 5 and VCF2 isoform 3 appear to increase the association of ubiquitylated substrates with p97.
source: By contrast, the more weakly expressed VCF1 isoform 5 and VCF2 isoform 3 did not interfere with binding of UFD1-NPL4 and p47 and even appeared to increase the association of ubiquitylated substrates with p97.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FAM104 proteins bind very tightly to p97.
source: These results suggest that FAM104 proteins bind very tightly to p97 and that their effect on cofactor and substrate binding depends on their expression level.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ability of overexpressed VCF1 to outcompete other cofactors.

claim: The effect of FAM104 proteins on cofactor and substrate binding depends on their expression level.
source: These results suggest that FAM104 proteins bind very tightly to p97 and that their effect on cofactor and substrate binding depends on their expression level.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of strongly versus weakly expressed VCF1/2 isoforms on cofactor binding.

claim: p97 homologs from yeast to mammals possess a relatively weak potential cNLS (residues K60-R65 in human p97, score 5 according to cNLS mapper).
source: p97 homologs from yeast to mammals possess a relatively weak potential cNLS (residues K60-R65 in human p97, score 5 according to cNLS mapper).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and cNLS prediction.

claim: An additional, functional bi-partite cNLS found closer to the N terminus in yeast Cdc48 is conserved in several p97 homologs from organisms lacking FAM104 proteins, but lost or poorly conserved in most p97 homologs from organisms possessing FAM104 proteins.
source: Interestingly, an additional, functional bi-partite cNLS found closer to the N terminus in yeast Cdc48 (Madeo et al., 1998) is conserved in several p97 homologs from organisms lacking FAM104 proteins, but lost or poorly conserved in most p97 homologs from organisms possessing FAM104 proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citation to Madeo et al., 1998.

claim: FAM104 proteins may compensate the loss of the functional bipartite cNLS in p97 homologs by exposing a very strong cNLS connected via a long, flexible region with the C-terminal helix tightly interacting with the p97 N domain.
source: This raises the intriguing possibility that FAM104 proteins compensate the loss of the functional bipartite cNLS in the latter p97 homologs by exposing a very strong cNLS that is connected via a long, flexible region with the C-terminal helix tightly interacting with the p97 N domain.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the correlation between FAM104 presence and cNLS conservation patterns.

claim: A model cargo of roughly the same size as the p97 hexamer (MS2S37P) had to be decorated with at least 10 NLSs for detectable nuclear import.
source: In a recent quantitative study, a model cargo of roughly the same size as the p97 hexamer, MS2S37P, had to be decorated with at least 10 NLSs for detectable nuclear import (Paci et al., 2020), suggesting that the six moderately strong and potentially masked cNLSs in the p97 hexamer are insufficient and have to be assisted by the strong cNLSs of VCF1/2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Paci et al., 2020.

claim: The six moderately strong and potentially masked cNLSs in the p97 hexamer are insufficient for efficient nuclear import and have to be assisted by the strong cNLSs of VCF1/2.
source: In a recent quantitative study, a model cargo of roughly the same size as the p97 hexamer, MS2S37P, had to be decorated with at least 10 NLSs for detectable nuclear import (Paci et al., 2020), suggesting that the six moderately strong and potentially masked cNLSs in the p97 hexamer are insufficient and have to be assisted by the strong cNLSs of VCF1/2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison with the model cargo study and the observed effects of VCF1/2 on p97 nuclear localization.

claim: Additional nuclear cofactors such as UBXN7 with its strong cNLS likely contribute to the efficient nuclear targeting of p97.
source: Since de(p)letion of VCF1/2 caused only a partial reduction in nuclear p97 levels in our experiments, it is likely that additional nuclear cofactors such as UBXN7 with its strong cNLS contribute to the efficient nuclear targeting of p97.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the partial reduction of nuclear p97 upon VCF1/2 loss.

claim: AKIRIN2 promotes the nuclear import of the assembled 20S proteasome.
source: Intriguingly, two other small proteins possessing strong NLSs were recently found to possess functions analogous to VCF1/2 in the nuclear import of essential protein complexes of the ubiquitin proteasome system. AKIRIN2 and HAPSTR1 promote the nuclear import of the assembled 20S proteasome (de Almeida et al., 2021) and of the E3 ligase HUWE1 (Monda et al., 2023), respectively, indicating that the decoration of protein complexes with small, NLS-containing interaction partners is a general strategy of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Almeida et al., 2021.

claim: HAPSTR1 promotes the nuclear import of the E3 ligase HUWE1.
source: Intriguingly, two other small proteins possessing strong NLSs were recently found to possess functions analogous to VCF1/2 in the nuclear import of essential protein complexes of the ubiquitin proteasome system. AKIRIN2 and HAPSTR1 promote the nuclear import of the assembled 20S proteasome (de Almeida et al., 2021) and of the E3 ligase HUWE1 (Monda et al., 2023), respectively, indicating that the decoration of protein complexes with small, NLS-containing interaction partners is a general strategy of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Monda et al., 2023.

claim: The decoration of protein complexes with small, NLS-containing interaction partners is a general strategy of cells.
source: Intriguingly, two other small proteins possessing strong NLSs were recently found to possess functions analogous to VCF1/2 in the nuclear import of essential protein complexes of the ubiquitin proteasome system. AKIRIN2 and HAPSTR1 promote the nuclear import of the assembled 20S proteasome (de Almeida et al., 2021) and of the E3 ligase HUWE1 (Monda et al., 2023), respectively, indicating that the decoration of protein complexes with small, NLS-containing interaction partners is a general strategy of cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the examples of AKIRIN2, HAPSTR1, and VCF1/2.

claim: VCF1 and VCF2 are broadly expressed in many human tissues, including strong expression in the brain.
source: According to the Human Protein Atlas and Proteomics DB databases, VCF1 and 2 are broadly expressed in many human tissues, including strong expression in the brain.
evidence: This claim is based on database information from the Human Protein Atlas and Proteomics DB.

claim: VCF1 has been implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis based on systematic yeast two-hybrid screening and computationally predicted neurodegenerative disease-associated protein clusters.
source: In this context, it is interesting to note that both proteins have recently been implicated in neurodegenerative diseases (VCF1: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; VCF2: Alzheimer's disease), based on systematic yeast two-hybrid screening and computationally predicted neurodegenerative disease-associated protein clusters (Haenig et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haenig et al., 2020.

claim: VCF2 has been implicated in Alzheimer's disease based on systematic yeast two-hybrid screening and computationally predicted neurodegenerative disease-associated protein clusters.
source: In this context, it is interesting to note that both proteins have recently been implicated in neurodegenerative diseases (VCF1: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; VCF2: Alzheimer's disease), based on systematic yeast two-hybrid screening and computationally predicted neurodegenerative disease-associated protein clusters (Haenig et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haenig et al., 2020.

claim: VCF1/2 may have a role in p97-dependent cancer cell survival.
source: Moreover, the potential link between VCF1/2 and p97-mediated DNA damage repair suggested by our data could hint to a role of VCF1/2 in p97-dependent cancer cell survival, an area of intense biomedical research efforts.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed involvement of VCF1/2 in p97 nuclear functions and DNA damage response.
